newsitem.title: USA: U.S. brokers seen being swept up in consolidation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. brokers seen being swept up in consolidation.

text.p: U.S. brokers and investment banks are likely to be swept up in a wave of industry consolidation that will probably continue unabated for the foreseeable future, analysts and traders said.
Heading the list of brokers rumored to be on the list of acquisition candidates are Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc, Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette, and Oppenheimer & Co.
"Everything is for sale in ths euphoric enviroment," said a trader who did not want to identified.

Asked if recent signs of softening in earnings reports at some brokers could deter buyers, the trader responded, "It's not an earnings issue. It's a question of the consolidation between banking and securities."

NationsBank Corp, a Charlotte, N.C.-based bank holding company with about $239 billion in assets, may be the latest to take a big plunge into brokerage. CNBC reported Thursday that announcement of a $1 billion deal to buy San Francisco-based Montgomery Securities was close at hand.

Asked for comment, a Mongtomery spokesman said the company has said in the past that it was considering sale of a stake but no announcement has been made. NationsBank officials were not immediately available for comment. Montgomery has been a big player in taking high-technology firms public.

Divided into separate segments of financial services in the 1930's, commercial banks on the one hand and brokers and investment banks on the other have been moving to take advantage of some relaxation of the restrictions that each faces upon entering on the other's turf.

But executives of securities firms say the playing field is tilted, with banks able to buy brokers but brokers not allowed to step in and buy banks. Efforts are under way in Washington to rewrite the depression-era laws, although the outcome is uncertain.
Among firms rumored to be up for sale, the hottest prospect at the moment may be Oppenheimer, which according to a source familiar with the situation is talking to Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.

Canadian Imperial, which owns the broker CIBC Wood Gundy, could have a better chance of making a deal than some others who looked at Oppenheimer. The existence of an experienced team of managers at CIBC Wood Gundy raises the chances the talks could lead to a deal, a source said.
A spokeswoman for CIBC Wood Gundy said, "I have no comment" about any oppeneheimer talks.
A spokesman for Lehman noted that over the last couple of years its response to rumors has been that it is building its business as an independent organization.

Oppenheimer, which is not connected with the similarly named mutual fund company, also declined to comment. A spokesman for Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette was not immediately available for comment. A spokesman for Equitable Cos Inc, which owns more than 70 percent of DLJ, said as it a matter of policy it does not comment on such speculation when asked if the stake might be for sale.
DLJ, long known for its institutional research, has emerged more recently as a major player in high-risk high-yield "junk" bonds. It is one of the biggest junk underwriters.

Speculation about sales of brokerage firms began to build up after Bankers Trust New York Corp announced in April it was going to buy Alex. Brown Inc for $1.7 billion, and BankAmerica Corp said earlier this month it would buy Robertson Stephens & Co for $540 million.

Earlier in the year, Morgan Stanley Group Inc, an investment bank catering mainly to big institutional investors, agreed to buy retail broker Dean Witter Discover & Co for $10.2 billion. That combination was completed at the end of May.

Dean WItter Discover officials said on Wednesday when the new firm reported its first quarterly earnings that the combination is already paying off by helping it land lead manager roles in key underwriting deals.

Perrin Long, an independent analyst who tracks the securities industry, said there could be one or two more deals where banks buy brokers. "I also think in addition we might see three or four deals where one securities firm takes over another," he said.

Long said NationsBank Corp, the Charlotte-N.C., based bank that has expanded its business all over the country through acquisitions, might buy a broker such as A.G. Edwards Inc. A spokesman for A.G. Edwards said the firm believes it can serve clients employees and shareholders best by remaining independent.

Chicago-based EVEREN Capital Corp is another retail-oriented broker that could attract a buyer, a trader said. In an interviw with Reuters in May, Everen chief executive James Boris said the company was interested in making acquisitions, alliances and joint ventures.

Another source said Travelers Group Inc, headed by Wall Street legend Sanford Weill, has a long history of successful acquisitions and could not be ruled out as a big player in the consolidation wave.
